reader.summary: Italy's week was shaped by growing social protest, an infrastructure scare, and a cluster of economic and diplomatic moves. Police clashed with demonstrators in Milan and Bologna, and TV5Monde described the unrest as a French-style contestation beginning to grip the country. A data-transmission failure forced Italian air traffic control to cut capacity in half, though the fault was repaired within the window and flights returned to normal. On the economic front, Rome secured an EU agreement to cap gas prices and pass savings on to electricity bills, while the three-year budget earmarked roughly 11 billion euros from financial-sector levies. UniCredit received ECB approval to take control of Germany's Commerzbank. PM Meloni publicly criticised Trump's diesel arrangement with Putin and his approach to Ukraine, calling the moves risky. Italy also prolonged its Schengen border suspension with Spain and opened a judicial probe into senior Israeli officials over the Gaza flotilla. The Pope's cancer diagnosis drew widespread reaction in Rome. In sport, Italian clubs suffered four Champions League defeats in two days, a painful run for the national game. Southern Italy faced potential fuel shortages as Ilva steelworkers' protests threatened an Eni refinery.

UniCredit and Commerzbank will move into early operational planning after the ECB approval, while the Israeli flotilla probe will draw a formal diplomatic response from Jerusalem. The air-traffic disruption will have fully receded from the headlines, and the Lombardy data-centre revision will add a smaller but concrete regulatory note.

crystal.summary: Next week in Italy, the protest movement that erupted in Milan and Bologna will spread to additional cities as unions and student groups add their voices, turning a regional flashpoint into a national contestation that Italian and French media will frame as a shared European pattern. The Vatican will issue medical updates on the Pope's cancer treatment, and the faithful will gather again in Rome, keeping the diagnosis at the centre of the country's conversation. Meloni and her cabinet will press their diplomatic case against the US-Russia diesel arrangement and Trump's Ukraine posture, likely drawing a sharper response from Washington and complicating Italy's standing within the alliance. The Eni refinery in southern Italy faces a real risk of shutdown as Ilva steelworkers tighten their blockade, which will force the government to act on fuel supplies. The air-traffic disruption that briefly halved flight capacity will exit the headlines entirely.

display.eli5:
Italy is having a rough week. Workers and students marched in Milan and Bologna, police got involved, and French TV channels are calling it a new wave of protest similar to what France is seeing. Next week this will probably spread to more cities and get bigger, so think of it as the protest story that won't go away.

At the same time, the Pope was diagnosed with cancer. People are praying outside a hospital in Rome, and next week the Vatican will probably share more details about his treatment. This is a big deal because the Pope is a global figure and Italians feel very close to him.

On the politics side, PM Meloni is publicly calling out President Trump over a diesel-fuel deal he made with Russia and his handling of the Ukraine war. Expect her government to keep talking tough, and Washington to talk back. That diplomatic spat will keep simmering.

The surprise to watch for is the steelworkers at the Ilva plant in the south. They are blocking an Eni oil refinery, and if it actually shuts down, southern Italy could run short on fuel. The government would have to jump in fast. That is the thing that would genuinely surprise most people.
